title: Sand in Medulin: 4 Myths About Bijeca and Its Beaches
metaDescription: Does Medulin have real sand? Bijeca is mixed sand and pebble; Kamenjak is mostly rock. Surfaces, shallow water, shade and parking for each beach.
content:
Medulin is one of the few places in Istria where sand is not a myth, but expectations need adjusting. Bijeca is a true sandy beach. It is not a Caribbean strip, and the rest of the municipality is pebble, rock and concrete.

## Myth 1: "Medulin has no sand, like the rest of Croatia"

**Reality:** Bijeca, in the centre of Medulin, is about 1 km long and has a sandy bottom with a very gradual entry into the sea. Water stays shallow for a long way out, so small children can paddle and build sandcastles without swimming skills. Its upper end changes to pebble.

**Better alternative:** Treat Bijeca as the answer for anyone who prioritises sand. It is a short walk from the town centre, and the promenade behind it leads to the small harbour. Most apartments in the centre are within walking distance, which removes the parking issue entirely.

## Myth 2: "Bijeca is sand from end to end"

**Reality:** Pebbles take over at the top end, and the sand is mixed with gravel in places. Trees behind the beach give some shade, but not enough to cover the whole strip. In July and August, the stretch nearest the centre fills first.

**Better alternative:** Walk away from the busiest section and pick the sandy middle for toddlers. Bring your own sun shelter, because tree shade goes quickly. Arrive before 10:00 in peak season. Drivers should use the paid car parks in Medulin, which fill by late morning in August; walking in from your accommodation is easier.

**Insider perspective:** The sandy part is also where the loungers, an aqua park and the crowds are. Families who want sand and quiet should go early or after 17:00.

## Myth 3: "Cape Kamenjak is the sandy beach everyone describes"

**Reality:** Kamenjak, near Premantura, is a protected nature park with about 30 km of coastline. The shore is mostly flat rock and pebble. Debeljak is often called sandy, but the sand is in the sea, while the beach itself is gravel and pebble with flat rock at the sides. Portić is the other bay usually mentioned for sandy bottom. Shade is limited, and there is no real infrastructure beyond a few bars.

**Better alternative:** Go to Kamenjak for clear water and scenery, not sand. Wear water shoes and bring an umbrella. It is roughly 15 minutes by car from Medulin. Parking is on dirt tracks inside the park, and an entrance fee applies, so check it at the gate.

## Myth 4: "Any beach near Medulin will work for small kids"

**Reality:** The bays around Pomer are fine gravel or pebble, and Centinera is a mix of pebble and rock. Rock shelves and concrete platforms are common along the coast, and entries are steeper than Bijeca's. These beaches suit swimmers and couples.

**Better alternative:** If Bijeca is too crowded, the next sandy option is Pješčana Uvala (Sandy Bay) in Pula, which has a playground and is about 15-20 minutes away by car. Further north, Bi Val in Fažana has some sandy patches, roughly 35 minutes by car. Levan, one of the Medulin islands, also has a small sandy beach, reached by excursion boat from Medulin.

## Myth 5: "Sand lovers should skip Medulin for Rab"

**Reality:** Rab has the larger sand beaches. Rajska Plaža at Lopar is about 1.5 to 2 km long and shallow, and Lopar has several other sandy bays. From Medulin, though, that is a full day of driving plus a ferry crossing, in practice around 4 hours each way. Mali Lošinj has sand-and-pebble bays and is similarly far.

**Better alternative:** Make Rab a destination in its own right, not a day trip from Medulin. For a normal Istria holiday, Bijeca covers the need.

**Opinionated take:** Do not drive to Kamenjak expecting sand under your towel, and do not pay for a long trip to Rab just to see more of it. Spend that day on Bijeca at 8:00, before the crowds.

## Is Medulin right if sand is the priority?

Yes, with limits. Medulin is the best base in Istria for families with small children who want shallow, sandy water, because Bijeca is walkable and the entry is gentle. It is not right for anyone expecting wide soft-sand beaches with shade everywhere, or sand along the whole coast. Beyond Bijeca, expect pebble, rock and concrete. Choose an apartment within walking distance of Bijeca, book for June or September if crowds matter, and treat Pješčana Uvala in Pula as the backup.

faq.question: But isn't Croatia all pebble, so Medulin can't have a real sandy beach?
faq.answer: Most of Croatia is pebble, but Bijeca in Medulin is a sandy beach about 1 km long with a very gradual entry. Its upper end turns to pebble, and nearly everything else around Medulin is pebble, rock or concrete.

faq.question: Is Bijeca beach good for toddlers?
faq.answer: Yes. The water stays shallow for a long way out and the bottom is sandy. Choose the sandy middle section, bring a sun shelter because shade is limited, and arrive before 10:00 in July and August.

faq.question: Is Cape Kamenjak a sandy beach?
faq.answer: Not really. It is mostly flat rock and pebble. Debeljak has sand in the sea, not on the shore. Water shoes are advisable, and shade is scarce.

faq.question: Where is the nearest sandy beach if Bijeca is full?
faq.answer: Pješčana Uvala in Pula is about 15-20 minutes by car and has a playground. Bi Val in Fažana is about 35 minutes away.

faq.question: Where are the nearest large sandy beaches in Croatia?
faq.answer: Rajska Plaža in Lopar on Rab is about 1.5 to 2 km long, and Mali Lošinj has sand-and-pebble bays. Both mean roughly 4 hours of travel from Medulin including a ferry, so they suit an overnight stay, not a day trip.

faq.question: Do I need a car to reach Bijeca?
faq.answer: No. It is in the centre of Medulin, and most accommodation in town is within walking distance. Parking nearby is paid and fills up by late morning in August.
